opus-5.5.text:
I think technical strategy is probably the most important thing for a company like ours, maybe more important than in almost any other kind of company. When you train foundation models, the cost of each decision is very high. One training run can take months of compute and a large share of your resources. If you bet on the wrong direction, you don't just lose the money. You lose time, and in this field time is very expensive because the frontier keeps moving.

So technical strategy is really about judging where the next bottleneck will be. A few years ago many people thought the main thing was scaling parameters. Then data became the constraint: how much high-quality data exists, and how to use it efficiently. Now a lot of the question is how to scale reinforcement learning, how to let models think longer, use tools, and act as agents over long horizons. Each phase needs a different bet, and you have to make it before the evidence is fully clear. If you wait until everyone agrees, it's already too late.

I also think strategy means deciding what not to do. A startup can't compete on every front with the largest companies. We have to concentrate resources on a few things where we believe we can be at the frontier, for example long context earlier on, and then reasoning and agentic capabilities. Focus is part of strategy.

Another part is the connection between strategy and organization. You need a team where researchers and engineers are tightly coupled, so an idea can go from a small experiment to a large training run quickly. A lot of the advantage comes from iteration speed, not from one brilliant idea. So the strategy has to include how you build infrastructure, how you evaluate, how you decide which experiments deserve to scale.

Finally, I think technical strategy should come from first principles rather than following others. It's tempting to look at what the leading labs publish and copy it, but by then they've already moved on. You have to ask yourself what is fundamentally true about intelligence and scaling, and build your roadmap from that. Sometimes you'll be wrong, but that's the only way to have a chance of being ahead.

r001.rationale: The response calls technical strategy probably the most important thing for a model-training company and says it may matter more there than in almost any other kind of company.

r002.rationale: It describes multiple shifting technical directions and says strategy requires choosing a few areas to pursue while deciding what not to do, because the company cannot compete on every front.

fable-5.1.text:
I think technical strategy is actually the core of the company, not something that sits on top of it. When you're training frontier models, almost every decision you make is a bet on where the technology is going over the next one, two, three years. And the thing about this field is that the bets are extremely expensive. A single training run can cost tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, and you only get a handful of those runs per year. So you can't afford to be wrong very often.

What that means in practice is that strategy and research can't be separated. In a traditional company you might have a strategy team that decides direction and an engineering team that executes. Here, the people making the strategic calls have to actually understand the technology at a very deep level, because the key questions are technical questions. Is scaling pretraining still the main lever, or is the leverage shifting to reinforcement learning and test-time compute? How much should you invest in long-context versus multimodal versus agentic capabilities? Those aren't questions you can answer by reading market reports. You answer them by looking at your own experiments and having a strong intuition about what the scaling curves are telling you.

The other thing I'd say is that technical strategy is really about focus. There are many promising directions, and a small team can't pursue all of them. The big labs have enough resources to try everything in parallel. We don't, so our edge has to come from picking the right few things and going much deeper on them than anyone else. Long context was an example of that for us early on. We believed it was fundamentally important, not just a feature, and we committed to it before it was consensus.

And finally, I think good technical strategy has to be honest about uncertainty. The field changes every few months. If you lock yourself into a plan and refuse to update, you'll be wrong very quickly. So we try to keep a clear long-term thesis about where things are going, like AGI being fundamentally about scaling and generalization, while staying flexible on the specific path to get there. The thesis gives you direction, the flexibility keeps you alive.

r001.rationale: Calling technical strategy “the core of the company” clearly presents it as the most important component for a model-training company.

r002.rationale: The response says many directions are promising and a small team cannot pursue them all, so choosing a few to focus on matters.

astra-6.text:
I think technical strategy is central to a company focused on training models, because you’re always making decisions under uncertainty. You have limited compute, limited people, and limited time. The question is which experiments will teach you the most, and which capabilities are worth investing in for the long term.

That means research direction and resource allocation have to be closely connected. If you believe data quality is the bottleneck, that should change where your team spends its effort. If you believe a different training approach could unlock a major improvement, you need a way to test that hypothesis before committing a large amount of compute.

So I see technical strategy as a set of hypotheses that you continually update through experiments. You need a clear direction, but you also need the discipline to change your mind when the evidence changes. The advantage comes from making that learning cycle faster and more reliable.

r001.rationale: Calling technical strategy “central” to a model-training company clearly conveys that it is a highly important part of company strategy.

r002.rationale: The response discusses choosing experiments and long-term investments, but does not communicate that the vast space of technical possibilities makes choosing which directions to pursue or forgo important.

sol-6.1.text:
I think technical strategy is really about deciding where to place your bets under uncertainty. For a company focused on training models, compute, data, and research talent are all limited, so you need a clear view of which investments will produce the most learning and, ultimately, the strongest capabilities.

That means connecting long-term research with day-to-day execution. Which ideas deserve a small experiment? Which results are strong enough to justify a much larger training run? And what infrastructure do you need so that the team can iterate quickly and trust the results?

You also have to connect those decisions to the product. A model can improve on a benchmark without becoming substantially more useful to users. So the strategy needs a feedback loop between research, training, and real use.

The important thing is to have a direction without becoming attached to a particular technical assumption. You make a judgment, test it, and update it as the evidence changes.

r001.rationale: The response describes technical strategy as important for allocating limited resources, but never suggests it may be the most important component of company strategy.

r002.rationale: It discusses choosing investments and experiments under uncertainty, but does not clearly explain that the vast range of technical possibilities makes choosing which directions to pursue or forgo important.
